doc.title: Bobby Shew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 1, 2020

title: Preparing to be eclectic; studio competition and cliques
summary: Shew urges students to learn every style, then describes how fast word of a chipped note spreads and why he left the studios in 1982.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Well yeah but I think the thing is you have to learn to think on your feet you know. And I mean I encourage the students that study with me now, especially if they’re in school, I’m caught in between two realities on this. One of them is being eclectic and learning to play all styles while you’re young. That means study classical music yes. Learn to double, triple tongue, yes. You know, learn to transpose, yes. If you have to play a C trumpet okay get one. Whatever. But become, you have to be prepared. And if you, you know a hundred percent doesn’t exist. Perfect doesn’t exist. But you walk into those situations out there in a studio and you’re just like the utility guy. You walk in not knowing what you’re going to run into and you have to just be ready for whatever can happen. And sometimes it just, like that situation with me with the alternate fingerings, whoo I don’t know how I managed to come up with that but the fact that I did saved my ass and saved my career. I mean I could have been really, you know once they say, there’s a funny little story I’ll give ya. The musicians are talking to a contractor and they say to the contractor, “Have you heard this new guy in town, Bobby Shew?” “No I haven’t heard him, no, no, never heard of him. What’s his name, Bobby Shew?” “Yeah, yeah. Oh yeah he’s quite a player. Yeah I was on a session with him last week and God he came in and sight read everything, he just played beautifully and lyrically and everything. And then I was on a session the next day and he was playing up in the upper register like Maynard, God I couldn’t believe it, everybody was saying wow this guy, Bobby Shew.” “What’s his name, Bobby Shew?” “Yeah you’ve got to know him.” No, the contractor had never heard of him, never heard of him. “And then a couple of days ago I was on a session and he chipped a high D.” “Oh I did hear about that.” You know and this is one of the things about the studio situation is that as long as you’re okay, you’re okay. But the minute you start chipping, the word’s all over town in a minute. I mean word gets out. And it’s so competitive, Monk, for every chair open for trumpet there’s 300 guys sitting there wishing they were on it. You know? And there’s a — all the contractors have priority lists. And sometimes some of the musicians, I won’t say any names here but one of the reasons I quit the studio in 1982 is because there were a couple of musicians that came in that were trying to control who was being called on sessions. And this one guy for instance, he would get a call from the service said well you’re such and such for such and such day and such and such hours. And he’d say, “Well who else is in the trumpet section?” “Well Bobby Shew and Dalton Smith.” “Really?
